title: The Cupbearer's Tears
subtitle: Nehemiah 1:1–11
description: A brother's report from Judah breaks a cupbearer's heart in Susa, and his prayer ends by asking for mercy in the sight of one particular man.
paragraphs: This book is a memoir, and it says so in its first line: “These are the words of Nehemiah son of Hacaliah.” Nehemiah dates his own story the way the whole return has been dated, by a Persian king's reign: in the month of Chislev, in the twentieth year, he was in the citadel of Susa, the same royal city where Esther's story had unfolded under the previous king. Jerusalem had a temple again, rebuilt two generations of the story earlier, and a company had gone up with Ezra under this same Artaxerxes. Then Nehemiah's brother arrived from Judah. His name was Hanani, and he came with men from Judah, and Nehemiah questioned them about the Jews who had survived the exile, and about Jerusalem.

The answer he got is quoted exactly as he records it: “The remnant who survived the exile are there in the province, in great trouble and disgrace.” And then the sentence the whole book turns on: “The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates have been burned with fire.” A city could have a temple and still stand open to anyone who wanted to walk in. Its people lived in disgrace in their own province, behind no wall, with burned gates lying where Nebuchadnezzar's armies had left them generations before. Nehemiah heard it in the citadel of the king of Persia, about as far from the rubble as a man could be while still calling it home.

His response came before any plan did. “When I heard these words, I sat down and wept.” He mourned for days, “fasting and praying before the God of heaven,” and the prayer he prayed is written out in full, because this book wants its readers to know what its governor said to God before he ever said anything to the king. It opens on who God is: “O LORD, God of heaven, the great and awesome God who keeps His covenant of loving devotion with those who love Him and keep His commandments.” Then it moves at once to confession, and the confession starts with the man praying it: “I confess the sins that we Israelites have committed against You.” “Both I and my father’s house have sinned.” No excuses are made for anyone, and none are made for himself.

The prayer then does something deliberate: it quotes God back to God. Nehemiah asked Him to remember the word He had spoken through Moses: “If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you among the nations,” but the same word carried a promise home: “but if you return to Me and keep and practice My commandments,” then “even if your exiles have been banished to the farthest horizon, I will gather them from there and bring them to the place I have chosen as a dwelling for My Name.” The people in trouble in the province were still, the prayer insists, God's own: “They are Your servants and Your people.” “You redeemed them by Your great power and mighty hand.”

So the prayer comes down to one request, and it is smaller and braver than it first sounds: “Give Your servant success this day, I pray, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man.” This man. The prayer does not name him, but the chapter's last line does the naming by telling us Nehemiah's job: “I was the cupbearer to the king.” The cupbearer tasted the king's wine before the king drank it, stood closer to Artaxerxes than almost anyone in the empire, and had no authority at all over a broken wall a thousand miles away. Whatever was going to happen for Jerusalem would have to begin with a cupbearer's face in front of a king, and Nehemiah had spent days on his knees preparing to risk exactly that.

title: The King's Question and the Night Ride
subtitle: Nehemiah 2:1–20
description: A sad face before the king, a prayer breathed in half a second, and a midnight ride around the ruins before a word is spoken to anyone.
paragraphs: Four months passed between the prayer and its answer. In the month of Nisan, still in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, wine was set before the king, and Nehemiah took the wine and gave it to him, doing the job he had always done. Only something showed that had never shown before: “I had never been sad in his presence.” The king saw it instantly. “Why is your face sad, though you are not ill?” he asked. “This could only be sadness of the heart.” A sad face in front of a Persian king could be read as discontent, and discontent at that court could be fatal. Nehemiah says it plainly: “I was overwhelmed with fear.”

He answered anyway, and his answer named the thing his prayer had been circling: “May the king live forever!” “Why should I not be sad when the city where my fathers are buried lies in ruins, and its gates have been destroyed by fire?” The king did not dismiss him. He asked the question the whole winter of prayer had been waiting for: “What is your request?” Nehemiah's memoir records what happened in the half second before he spoke, and it became one of the most remembered lines in the book: “So I prayed to the God of heaven.” Then, out loud, to the king: “If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor in your sight,” “I ask that you send me to Judah, to the city where my fathers are buried, so that I may rebuild it.” The queen was seated beside the king when he asked the practical question: “How long will your journey take, and when will you return?” It pleased the king to send him, and Nehemiah set a time.

Leave of absence was only the first request. Nehemiah asked for letters to the governors west of the Euphrates, so the empire's own officials would grant him safe passage to Judah, and a letter to Asaph, keeper of the king's forest, ordering timber “to make beams for the gates of the citadel to the temple, for the city wall, and for the house I will occupy.” The result is given in the sentence Ezra's memoir also runs on, word for word the same confession from the other man's book: “And because the gracious hand of my God was upon me, the king granted my requests.” He made the journey with the king's letters in his hand and the king's army officers and cavalry riding with him, and delivered the letters to the governors. Not everyone was pleased that he had come. Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite official heard of it, and the memoir records their reaction exactly: they were “deeply disturbed that someone had come to seek the well-being of the Israelites.”

Nehemiah had been in Jerusalem three days before he moved, and when he moved it was at night, with a few men, telling no one. “I did not tell anyone what my God had laid on my heart to do for Jerusalem.” The only animal with him was the one he rode. Out through the Valley Gate, toward the Well of the Serpent and the Dung Gate, he inspected the broken walls and the burned gates by darkness. At the Fountain Gate and the King's Pool, the rubble was so deep that “there was no room for the animal under me to get through,” so he went up the valley on foot, still inspecting, and came back in through the Valley Gate. He had walked the whole ruin himself before he said a word to anyone in the city. The officials did not know where he had gone or what he was doing.

Then he told them. He gathered the Jews, priests, nobles, and officials and said what the night ride had confirmed: “You see the trouble we are in. Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned down.” Then the call: “Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace.” He told them about the gracious hand of his God upon him, and what the king had said to him, and their answer came back immediate: “Let us start rebuilding.” The memoir adds that they set their hands to this good work. The opposition answered just as fast. Sanballat and Tobiah, now joined by Geshem the Arab, “mocked us and ridiculed us, saying,” “What is this you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?” Nehemiah's reply closes the chapter and sets the terms for everything that follows: “The God of heaven is the One who will grant us success.” “We, His servants, will start rebuilding, but you have no portion, right, or claim in Jerusalem.”

title: Every Family at the Wall
subtitle: Nehemiah 3:1–32
description: The record of the builders, gate by gate: priests and perfumers, a ruler's daughters, and the nobles who would not stoop.
paragraphs: The memoir pauses here and opens a record instead. Chapter 3 is not a story Nehemiah tells but a roster he kept: who rebuilt which gate, which stretch of wall, in what order, walking the whole circuit of the city from the Sheep Gate back to the Sheep Gate. The telling follows the record around the wall, because the record itself is the point. A broken city was being rebuilt by named people, and Nehemiah wrote down their names. It begins at the place of honor. “Eliashib the high priest and his fellow priests began rebuilding.” They dedicated the Sheep Gate and installed its doors, and built on as far as the Tower of the Hundred and the Tower of Hananel, dedicating that stretch too. Priests first, with their hands in the stonework. Next to them built the men of Jericho, a town down in the valley that had sent its men up to work on a wall that was not theirs.

From the Fish Gate the record runs hand to hand, family by family: “The Fish Gate was rebuilt by the sons of Hassenaah.” “They laid its beams and installed its doors, bolts, and bars.” Meremoth made repairs, and Meshullam, and Zadok. Then come the Tekoites, men of Tekoa, and the record keeps one sharp note about their town: the men worked, “but their nobles did not put their shoulders to the work under their supervisors.” It is the only rebuke in the chapter, and Nehemiah let it stand in writing. The Jeshanah Gate was repaired, and men of Gibeon and Mizpah took their sections, towns again sending workers to a city that was not their own.

What strikes you, reading the roster whole, is who is on this wall. Uzziel was “one of the goldsmiths.” Hananiah was “one of the perfumers.” Men who worked in precious metal and scented oil by trade are laying stones as far as the Broad Wall. Rulers of half-districts of Jerusalem built beside common families. Jedaiah made repairs across from his own house. And one line has stopped readers for as long as the book has been read: “Shallum son of Hallohesh, ruler of the other half-district of Jerusalem, made repairs, with the help of his daughters.” In a record of sons and fathers, one man's daughters are on the wall beside him, and Nehemiah wrote it down.

The circuit runs on. Hanun and the residents of Zanoah rebuilt the Valley Gate and “repaired a thousand cubits of the wall as far as the Dung Gate.” Malchijah, a district ruler, took the Dung Gate itself, the city's lowliest exit. Shallun roofed the Fountain Gate and repaired the wall by the Pool of Shelah, near the king's garden, down to the stairs from the City of David. Beyond him worked another man named Nehemiah, Nehemiah son of Azbuk, a district ruler, up to the tombs of David. Then the Levites under Rehum. Then Keilah's two half-districts, each under its own ruler, Hashabiah and Binnui. Then Ezer of Mizpah at the ascent to the armory, and Baruch, of whom the record says a little more: Baruch “diligently repaired another section,” all the way to the high priest's house.

The last stretch comes home around the east side. Priests from the surrounding area. Benjamin and Hasshub in front of their house. The temple servants living on the hill of Ophel, opposite the Water Gate. The Tekoites again, a second section, from the great tower to the wall of Ophel; their town appears twice in this record, and their nobles not once. Above the Horse Gate, “each of the priests made repairs in front of his own house.” Zadok built opposite his house. Shemaiah, the guard of the East Gate, built on the gate he guarded. Malchijah, a goldsmith, built as far as the Inspection Gate. And between the corner and the Sheep Gate, where the record began, “the goldsmiths and merchants made repairs.” The wall was not built by an army or a contractor. It was built section by section by the people who would have to live behind it, and the memoir keeps every name.

title: Mocked, Prayed, and Armed
subtitle: Nehemiah 4:1–23
description: A fox joke, a conspiracy, and a workforce rebuilt as a garrison, building with a weapon in one hand.
paragraphs: The laughter started as soon as the building did. When Sanballat heard the wall was going up, the memoir says he “was furious and filled with indignation,” and he performed his contempt in front of an audience, “before his associates and the army of Samaria.” The speech is recorded: “What are these feeble Jews doing?” Could they restore it themselves, finish in a day, offer sacrifices? “Can they bring these burnt stones back to life from the mounds of rubble?” Tobiah the Ammonite, standing beside him, added the line meant to be repeated: “If even a fox were to climb up on what they are building, it would break down their wall of stones!” Mockery was the first weapon used against the wall, and it was aimed at morale, at the picture the builders had of their own work.

Nehemiah answered the mockery the way he had answered the bad news from Judah, on his knees, and the prayer is as blunt as the insult: “Hear us, O God, for we are despised.” “Turn their scorn back upon their own heads, and let them be taken as plunder to a land of captivity.” He asked God not to cover up their sin, “for they have provoked the builders.” Then the prayer ended and the building went on, and the next sentence measures what the mockery failed to do: “So we rebuilt the wall until all of it was joined together up to half its height,” the whole circuit closed at half height, and the record gives the reason in six words: “for the people had a mind to work.”

Laughter failing, the opposition moved to conspiracy. Sanballat and Tobiah, with the Arabs, the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites, heard the gaps were closing and “conspired to come and fight against Jerusalem.” Nehemiah's response is the book's pattern in a single line, worth reading slowly: “So we prayed to our God and posted a guard against them day and night.” Prayer and a guard, both, neither instead of the other. But the pressure was telling inside the wall as well. The people of Judah had begun to sing their exhaustion: “The strength of the laborer fails, and there is so much rubble that we will never be able to rebuild the wall.” The enemy's plan was spoken where it could be overheard: “Before they know or see a thing, we will come into their midst, kill them, and put an end to the work.” And the Jews living near the enemy kept coming in with the same warning, ten times over: “Wherever you turn, they will attack us.”

So the work was reorganized as a defense. Nehemiah stationed men behind the lowest sections of the wall, at the exposed places, stationed by families, “with their swords, spears, and bows.” Then he inspected the line and stood up and said to the nobles, the officials, and the rest of the people: “Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons and your daughters, your wives and your homes.” The enemies heard the scheme was known, and that God had frustrated it, and every man went back to his section. But the work never went back to peacetime. From that day, half of Nehemiah's servants worked while the other half held “spears, shields, bows, and armor,” with the officers standing behind the people. “The laborers who carried materials worked with one hand and held a weapon with the other.” Every builder worked with his sword strapped at his side, and the trumpeter stayed beside Nehemiah.

The standing orders closed the chapter. “The work is great and extensive, and we are spread out far from one another along the wall.” So one signal covered the whole circuit: “Wherever you hear the sound of the horn, rally to us there. Our God will fight for us!” Half the men held spears “from the break of dawn until the stars came out.” Every man and his servant spent the night inside Jerusalem, guarding by night and working by day, so the countryside families stopped commuting through ambush country. And the memoir's last detail is about its own author: “neither I nor my brothers nor my servants nor the guards with me changed out of our clothes.” Each man carried his weapon, Nehemiah writes, even to go for water. The wall at half height had become a garrison that built.

title: The Outcry of the Poor
subtitle: Nehemiah 5:1–19
description: The famine inside the wall: fields mortgaged, children enslaved, a shaken robe, and a governor who would not eat the governor's bread.
paragraphs: The wall's worst threat did not come from Sanballat. About that time, the memoir says, there was “a great outcry from the people and their wives against their fellow Jews.” Famine was on the land, and the poor of Judah were being eaten by the rich of Judah while both worked on the same wall. The outcry came in three voices, and Nehemiah records all three. First, hunger: “We and our sons and daughters are numerous. We must get grain in order to eat and stay alive.” Then debt: “We are mortgaging our fields, our vineyards, and our homes to get grain during the famine.” Then the state's share: “We have borrowed money to pay the king’s tax on our fields and vineyards.” And underneath all of it, the thing that could not be unsaid once heard: “We and our children are just like our countrymen and their children, yet we are subjecting our sons and daughters to slavery.” Some of their daughters were already enslaved, and the parents were “powerless to redeem them because our fields and vineyards belong to others.”

Nehemiah's response has a sequence, and the memoir is careful to give it in order. First: “When I heard their outcry and these complaints, I became extremely angry.” Then, and the text marks the pause, “after serious thought” he acted. He rebuked the nobles and the officials to their faces: “You are exacting usury from your own brothers!” He called a large assembly against them and laid out the contradiction at the center of the return. The community had been buying back its own people from foreign slavery: “We have done our best to buy back our Jewish brothers who were sold to foreigners, but now you are selling your own brothers, that they may be sold back to us!” Against that sentence the nobles had nothing. The memoir records it flatly: “But they remained silent, for they could find nothing to say.”

He pressed on: “What you are doing is not right.” “Shouldn’t you walk in the fear of our God to avoid the reproach of our foreign enemies?” Then he put himself inside the charge before putting them under it. He and his brothers and his servants had also been lending money and grain to the people. “Please, let us stop this usury.” And the remedy was not an apology but restitution, immediately: “Please restore to them immediately their fields, vineyards, olive groves, and houses,” along with the percentage of money, grain, new wine, and oil that had been assessed on the loans. The nobles answered: “We will restore it,” “and will require nothing more from them. We will do as you say.” Nehemiah did not take the words alone. He summoned the priests and put the nobles and officials under oath to do what they had promised, and then he acted out the oath's curse in front of the assembly, shaking out the folds of his robe: “May God likewise shake out of his house and possessions every man who does not keep this promise.” The whole assembly answered Amen, and praised the LORD, and the record adds the sentence that matters: the people did as they had promised.

Then the memoir turns its testimony on its own author, because Nehemiah knew his demand would invite the question of what the governor himself took. From the day Artaxerxes appointed him governor in Judah, from the king's twentieth year to his thirty-second, twelve years in all, “neither I nor my brothers ate the food allotted to the governor.” The governors before him had burdened the people, “taking from them bread and wine plus forty shekels of silver,” and their servants had oppressed the people too. His own explanation is given in his own words: “But I did not do this, because of my fear of God.” Instead he devoted himself to the wall, gathered all his servants to the work, and acquired no land. His table fed the province at his own cost: “There were 150 Jews and officials at my table,” besides the guests who came from the surrounding nations, and every day one ox, six choice sheep, and fowl were prepared, with an abundance of wine every ten days. “I did not demand the food allotted to the governor, because the burden on the people was so heavy.”

The chapter closes with the first sounding of the prayer this book will end on, the governor's private signature set into the public record: “Remember me favorably, O my God, for all that I have done for this people.” Read the chapter whole and its shape is plain. The wall outside was at half height and rising; the community inside was consuming itself, field by field and child by child. Nehemiah treated the second as the emergency it was. A wall around a people who enslaved each other would only have made a stronger prison, and he seems to have known it. So the famine chapter stands in the middle of the building chapters, where he put it, between the armed builders and the finished wall.

title: I Cannot Come Down
subtitle: Nehemiah 6:1–19
description: Four invitations, an unsealed letter, a hired prophet, and a wall finished in fifty-two days.
paragraphs: The wall was finished except for its doors. Not a gap was left, though Nehemiah notes carefully that “to that time I had not yet installed the doors in the gates.” That is when the invitations began. Sanballat and Geshem sent a message, reasonable on its face: “Come, let us meet together in one of the villages on the plain of Ono.” A conference, on neutral ground, a day's walk from the city. Nehemiah read it for what it was: “But they were planning to harm me.” His answer became the most quoted sentence he ever sent: “I am doing a great work and cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it to go down to you?” The memoir notes the rhythm without decoration: “Four times they sent me the same message, and each time I gave the same reply.”

The fifth attempt changed weapons. Sanballat's servant came carrying an unsealed letter, a letter anyone along the road could read, which was the point. Its charges are reported here as what they were, the letter's words and not the truth. “It is reported among the nations,” it began, “you and the Jews are plotting to revolt, and this is why you are building the wall.” “According to these reports, you are to become their king, and you have even appointed prophets in Jerusalem to proclaim on your behalf:” “There is a king in Judah.” Then the hook: “Soon these rumors will reach the ears of the king. So come, let us confer together.” Treason, whispered to the whole road, with an offer to help hush it up. Nehemiah's reply denied nothing elaborately and conceded nothing at all: “There is nothing to these rumors you are spreading; you are inventing them in your own mind.” He knew the aim, and states it: they wanted the builders frightened into weakness, saying, “Their hands will be weakened in the work, and it will never be finished.” His whole counterattack is one short prayer: “But now, my God, strengthen my hands.”

The last plot came dressed as prophecy and concern for his life. Shemaiah, a man confined to his house, urged Nehemiah to hide with him: “Let us meet at the house of God inside the temple. Let us shut the temple doors because they are coming to kill you,” and then, repeated with the knife in it: “by night they are coming to kill you!” It sounded like rescue. Nehemiah heard it as a trap, and his refusal is the memoir at its most personal: “Should a man like me run away? Should one like me go into the temple to save his own life? I will not go!” A governor hiding unlawfully in the temple would have destroyed himself more surely than any assassin. Nehemiah saw through it in the moment: “I realized that God had not sent him,” but that Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him, hired to frighten the governor into a sin that would give him a bad name and discredit him. His answer to that plot, too, was a prayer, aimed the other way: “O my God, remember Tobiah and Sanballat for what they have done,” and Noadiah the prophetess and the other prophets who had tried to intimidate him.

Then, in one level sentence, the thing the whole book has been driving at: “So the wall was completed in fifty-two days, on the twenty-fifth of Elul.” Fifty-two days from rubble heaps and a fox joke to a finished circuit with gates. The verdict of the watching nations is recorded as the builders' own vindication: when the enemies heard of it, “all the surrounding nations were afraid and disheartened, for they realized that this task had been accomplished by our God.” The speed was the sermon. Nobody who had watched the work believed those feeble Jews, as Sanballat called them, had done it unaided in fifty-two days.

But the memoir refuses to end the opposition story at the wall's completion, because the opposition had a second front that stone could not close. In those same days, the nobles of Judah were writing letters to Tobiah, and Tobiah's letters kept coming to them. Many in Judah were bound by oath to him by marriage: Tobiah was son-in-law to Shecaniah, and his son had married the daughter of Meshullam, the same Meshullam who had repaired two sections of the wall. “Moreover, these nobles kept reporting to me Tobiah’s good deeds, and they relayed my words to him.” Every word the governor spoke was being carried to the enemy by men inside his own council, and Tobiah kept sending letters to intimidate him. The wall was finished. The harder sieges were still to come.

title: A City to Fill, and the Register
subtitle: Nehemiah 7:1–73
description: Guards at the gates, an empty city, and the old register of the first return found and opened for a new purpose.
paragraphs: With the wall rebuilt and its doors set in place, the gatekeepers, singers, and Levites were appointed to their posts, and Nehemiah set the city's government in order. He put his brother Hanani in charge of Jerusalem, the brother whose report had started everything, together with Hananiah the commander of the fortress, chosen for a stated reason: “he was a faithful man who feared God more than most.” Then came the standing orders for a city still surrounded by enemies. “Do not open the gates of Jerusalem until the sun is hot.” While the guards were on duty the doors were to stay shut and fastened, and the residents themselves were appointed as guards, some at fixed posts and some at their own homes. A finished wall was not a finished defense until disciplined men held it at the right hours.

Then Nehemiah names the problem the wall could not solve: “Now the city was large and spacious, but there were few people in it, and the houses had not yet been rebuilt.” Jerusalem was a defended shell, wide streets and empty lots inside a strong circuit, most of the province's people still living in their own towns. A capital needs inhabitants. So the memoir records where the plan came from, in its usual way: “Then my God put it into my heart to assemble the nobles, the officials, and the people to be enrolled by genealogy.” And looking for the roll of the people, Nehemiah found an old document: “I found the genealogical register of those who had first returned.”

Here the memoir opens that register and prints it, and readers of this series have seen it before: it is the roll of Zerubbabel's company from Ezra's book, the families who came up from Babylon in the first return under Cyrus. It is not read out again in this telling; Ezra's episodes carry it in full. What matters in Nehemiah's book is that the register exists, that it was kept, and that a governor ninety years later could open it to count the people he meant to settle in his empty city. It opens with the first return's leaders, Zerubbabel and Jeshua at their head, and among the names that follow stands an earlier Nehemiah, a leader of that first company, not the governor who found the list. Family by family the register runs: the sons of Parosh and Elam and Zattu, the men of Bethlehem and Jericho and Lod, the priests of Jedaiah and Immer and Pashhur, the Levites, the singers of Asaph, the gatekeepers, the temple servants, the descendants of Solomon's servants.

The register keeps its hard edges, and the telling keeps them too. Some who came up “could not prove that their families were descended from Israel,” and certain priestly families fared worse: “These men searched for their family records, but they could not find them and so were excluded from the priesthood as unclean.” The governor of that first day, the register says, suspended their case rather than settling it: “The governor ordered them not to eat the most holy things until there was a priest to consult the Urim and Thummim.” The roll closes with the count the whole series has now met twice: “The whole assembly numbered 42,360,” besides 7,337 menservants and maidservants and 245 singers, and it remembers the gifts that built the first temple fund, the heads of families giving darics of gold and minas of silver and priestly garments into the treasury.

One seam deserves to be named plainly, the way this series names them. In a number of families, this printing of the register counts differently than Ezra's printing of the same list. Neither book corrects the other, and this telling does not either; both stand as printed, and on the figure that matters most, the whole assembly, the two printings agree exactly: 42,360. The register's last line says the first company “settled in their own towns,” and that “by the seventh month the Israelites had settled in their towns.” Nehemiah now had his roll. The seventh month was coming again, and this time the people would gather inside a walled city, and what they asked for was not stone.

title: Ezra Reads the Law
subtitle: Nehemiah 8:1–18
description: A platform in the square, six hours of reading, weeping turned to feasting, and booths built for the first time since Joshua.
paragraphs: For this chapter the memoir steps back, and another man comes forward. When the seventh month came, all the people gathered together in the square before the Water Gate, inside the wall they had just finished, and the request that opened the day came from the people themselves: “they asked Ezra the scribe to bring out the Book of the Law of Moses.” Ezra's own story, the scribe who set his heart to study the Law and practice it and teach it, stands in his own book in this series. Here, in Nehemiah's memoir, he appears at the height of that life's work. On the first day of the seventh month, Ezra the priest brought the Law before the assembly, men and women and all who could listen and understand. “So Ezra read it aloud from daybreak until noon” as he faced the square. Six hours of reading, and the record of the crowd is one sentence: “And all the people listened attentively to the Book of the Law.”

Everything about the day was built for hearing. “Ezra the scribe stood on a high wooden platform built for this occasion,” with six men standing at his right and seven at his left. “Ezra opened the book in full view of all the people,” since he was standing above them all, “and as he opened it, all the people stood up.” Then Ezra blessed the LORD, the great God, and with their hands uplifted all the people answered Amen, Amen, and bowed down and worshiped with their faces to the ground. The Levites spread out among the crowd and instructed the people as they stood in their places. Reading alone was not the plan; understanding was: “So they read from the Book of the Law of God, explaining it and giving insight, so that the people could understand what was being read.”

Understanding, when it came, hurt. As the words were made plain, the people began to weep, hearing in the Law the measure of their own lives and their fathers' lives. Three voices stopped the weeping, the governor's among them. “Nehemiah the governor, Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who were instructing the people said to all of them, ‘This day is holy to the LORD your God. Do not mourn or weep.’” The record explains: “For all the people were weeping as they heard the words of the Law.” Then Nehemiah spoke the sentence the day is remembered by: “Go and eat what is rich, drink what is sweet, and send out portions to those who have nothing prepared, since today is holy to our Lord.” “Do not grieve, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.” The Levites calmed the crowd with the same word: “Be still, since today is holy. Do not grieve.” So the people went and ate and drank and sent out portions and rejoiced greatly. The record gives their reason, and it is not that they had been excused: it is that “they understood the words that had been made known to them.”

The next day the heads of the families came back with the priests and Levites and gathered around Ezra to study the words of the Law, and study turned up something the calendar required immediately. “And they found written in the Law, which the LORD had commanded through Moses, that the Israelites were to dwell in booths during the feast of the seventh month.” The feast was that month, days away. A proclamation went through the towns and Jerusalem: “Go out to the hill country and bring back branches of olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm, and other leafy trees, to make booths, as it is written.” The people went out and built them, on their rooftops, in their courtyards, in the courts of the house of God, in the squares by the Water Gate and the Gate of Ephraim, a city roofed in branches inside its new wall.

The record's verdict on the feast is measured against the whole history of Israel: “The whole assembly that had returned from exile made booths and lived in them.” “From the days of Joshua son of Nun until that day, the Israelites had not celebrated like this.” “And there was great rejoicing.” And through the feast the reading never stopped: “Day after day, from the first day to the last, Ezra read from the Book of the Law of God.” They kept the feast seven days, and on the eighth day held an assembly according to the ordinance. The wall had taken fifty-two days to build. It took the book one morning to fill the city inside it, first with grief that was answered, then with a joy the people were commanded not to apologize for.

title: The Great Confession
subtitle: Nehemiah 9:1–38
description: Sackcloth and dust, and the whole history of Israel prayed back to God by the Levites, ending here we are as slaves.
paragraphs: Three weeks after the reading came the reckoning. On the twenty-fourth day of the same month, the Israelites gathered again, this time “fasting and wearing sackcloth, with dust on their heads.” Those of Israelite descent separated themselves from the foreigners among them, and they stood and confessed, the record says, “their sins and the iniquities of their fathers.” The day was divided like the first one: “they read from the Book of the Law of the LORD their God for a quarter of the day, and they spent another quarter of the day in confession and worship of the LORD their God.” Then the Levites stood on their platform and cried out in a loud voice, and the Levites called the people up into the longest prayer in the book: “Stand up and bless the LORD your God from everlasting to everlasting:” “Blessed be Your glorious name, and may it be exalted above all blessing and praise.”

The prayer is Israel's whole history told back to God by the people who had just heard the Law read, and it begins before Israel exists. “You alone are the LORD.” He made the heavens and the earth and the seas and all that is in them: “You give life to all things, and the host of heaven worships You.” Then Abram, chosen and brought out of Ur of the Chaldeans and given the name Abraham. “You found his heart faithful before You,” and made a covenant to give his descendants the land of the Canaanites and Hittites and Amorites, and the prayer's first verdict falls: “You have kept Your promise, because You are righteous.” Then Egypt. He saw the affliction, heard the cry at the Red Sea, did signs and wonders against Pharaoh, who had acted with arrogance. “You made a name for Yourself that endures to this day.” He divided the sea, and hurled the pursuers into the depths like a stone into raging waters.

The wilderness takes the prayer's center, as it took Israel's life. He led them with a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night. “You came down on Mount Sinai and spoke with them from heaven.” He gave just ordinances and true laws, revealed His holy Sabbath, fed them bread from heaven in their hunger and brought water from the rock in their thirst, and told them to go in and possess the land. “But they and our fathers became arrogant and stiff-necked and did not obey Your commandments.” They refused to listen, forgot the wonders, stiffened their necks, and appointed a leader to take them back to bondage in Egypt. They cast a calf and said it had brought them up out of Egypt. And against all of it the prayer sets one sentence, the sentence the whole history hangs on: “But You are a forgiving God, gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and rich in loving devotion, and You did not forsake them.” “You in Your great compassion did not forsake them in the wilderness.” “For forty years You sustained them in the wilderness, so that they lacked nothing.”

Then the land, and the pattern that ruled it. He gave them kingdoms and peoples, Sihon of Heshbon and Og of Bashan, multiplied their descendants like the stars of heaven, and brought them into the land. They took fortified cities and fertile land, houses full of goods and wells already dug, and “they ate and were filled; they grew fat and delighted in Your great goodness.” Then they rebelled. They flung His law behind their backs and killed His prophets who warned them. So He delivered them into the hands of enemies, and in distress they cried, and from heaven He heard, and in compassion He gave them deliverers. Rest came, and evil came with rest, and dominion, and crying, and deliverance, “many times in Your compassion.” He was patient for many years, His Spirit admonishing them through the prophets, until He gave them into the hands of the neighboring peoples. The prayer will not let even the exile be the last word about Him: “But in Your great compassion, You did not put an end to them; nor did You forsake them, for You are a gracious and compassionate God.”

And then the prayer turns its face to the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month, inside a rebuilt wall in a Persian province, and renders its verdict on the whole story: “You are just in all that has befallen us, because You have acted faithfully, while we have acted wickedly.” Kings and leaders and priests and fathers are all named inside the guilt; no generation is excused and the present one does not excuse itself. The confession ends on the bitter irony of their address: “So here we are today as slaves in the land You gave our fathers to enjoy its fruit and goodness”: “here we are as slaves!” Its harvest goes to kings set over them because of their sins, who rule over their bodies and their livestock as they please. “We are in great distress.” And a confession that honest produced more than words. The prayer's last line announces a document: in view of all this, “we make a binding agreement, putting it in writing and sealing it” with the names of their leaders, Levites, and priests. The next sound in the book is a seal being pressed into wax.

title: Sealed with Names
subtitle: Nehemiah 10:1–39
description: The covenant in writing: marriages, Sabbath, debts, wood, firstfruits, and tithes, under one resolve, not to neglect the house of God.
paragraphs: The confession of the twenty-fourth day became a covenant on paper, and the paper survives with its signatures. The list of those who sealed the document runs for most of the chapter, priests first, then Levites, then the leaders of the people, and this telling frames it the way the memoir's other lists were framed, by its first name. The first seal on the agreement is the governor's own: “Nehemiah the governor, son of Hacaliah.” After the names, the covenant widens past the signers. “The rest of the people,” priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, temple servants, everyone who had separated themselves to obey the Law of God, with their wives and every son and daughter old enough to understand, “hereby join with their noble brothers and commit themselves with a sworn oath to follow the Law of God given through His servant Moses,” “and to obey carefully all the commandments, ordinances, and statutes of the LORD our Lord.” A curse stood behind the oath. These were the terms they swore to.

The first term guards the community's marriages: “We will not give our daughters in marriage to the people of the land, and we will not take their daughters for our sons.” The second guards the Sabbath, and it is specific enough to picture: “When the people of the land bring merchandise or any kind of grain to sell on the Sabbath day, we will not buy from them on a Sabbath or holy day.” No trade at all, not even the convenient kind. The third reaches into the fields and the debt books: “Every seventh year we will let the fields lie fallow and will cancel every debt.” Land rested, debts released, on a schedule written into an oath in a province that lived close to hunger. That clause alone would cost every signer something measurable.

The rest of the covenant funds the house of God, deliberately and in detail. They placed themselves under obligation to give a third of a shekel yearly “for the service of the house of our God,” a temple tax to cover the showbread, the regular grain offerings and burnt offerings, the Sabbath offerings, the New Moons and appointed feasts, the holy offerings, the sin offerings “to make atonement for Israel, and for all the duties of the house of our God.” Even the firewood was sworn for: “We have cast lots among the priests, Levites, and people for the donation of wood,” each family bringing its wood at its appointed time of year, “to burn on the altar of the LORD our God, as it is written in the Law.” Nothing about the temple's daily running was left to enthusiasm. It was budgeted, scheduled, and signed.

Then the firstfruits and the tithes, the covenant's supply lines. Firstfruits of the land and of every fruit tree, brought to the house of the LORD year by year. The firstborn of their sons and their livestock, and the firstborn of herds and flocks, brought to the priests who minister there. The firstfruits of their dough, their grain offerings, the fruit of all their trees, new wine and oil, carried to the priests at the storerooms. And the tithe itself, with its chain of custody spelled out: “A tenth of our produce belongs to the Levites, so that they shall receive tithes in all the towns where we labor.” A priest of Aaron's line would accompany the Levites when they collected it, and the Levites would bring a tenth of the tithes up to the storerooms of the treasury in the house of God. The singers and gatekeepers and ministering priests who had just been appointed to their posts in the finished city would be fed by this oath or not at all.

The agreement's last sentence is its purpose stated in nine words, and the rest of the book should be read against it: “Thus we will not neglect the house of our God.” Hold the terms up in a row and you hold the table of contents of everything that will go wrong and be fought for in the chapters left. Marriages with the peoples of the land. Buying on the Sabbath. The Levites' portions and the storerooms of the house. The covenant named its own battlegrounds in advance, in writing, under oath, with the governor's name sealed first. What a signed oath can hold, and what it cannot, is what the end of Nehemiah's book is about.

title: One of Ten, and Two Choirs
subtitle: Nehemiah 11:1–12:47
description: The lot that filled the city, and two thanksgiving choirs circling the finished wall in opposite directions to meet in the house of God.
paragraphs: A walled city with too few people in it is a fortress waiting to fall, so the leaders of the people settled in Jerusalem themselves, and the rest of the people solved the problem by lot. They cast lots “to bring one out of ten to live in the holy city of Jerusalem, while the remaining nine were to dwell in their own towns.” One family in ten would leave its land and its livelihood and move inside the circuit of the new wall, into a capital still half rebuilt, surrounded by enemies who had tried four times to stop the work. It was not a prize. The record shows it knew that: “And the people blessed all the men who volunteered to live in Jerusalem.” Men who were chosen, and men who stepped forward before the lot could choose them, were blessed by the neighbors who got to stay home.

The record of who settled runs long, and this telling frames it as the memoir's lists have been framed, by its shape and its totals. From Judah, the descendants of Perez in the city numbered 468 men of valor. From Benjamin, 928 men followed Sallu, under Joel son of Zichri. The priests who did the work of the temple numbered 822, with 242 leaders of families and 128 mighty men of valor beside them. The Levites in the holy city totaled 284, Mattaniah of Asaph's line leading in thanksgiving and prayer among them. The gatekeepers who kept watch at the gates were 172. The temple servants lived on the hill of Ophel. One name in the list faces the other direction, toward Persia: Pethahiah, “the king’s agent in every matter concerning the people,” the province's man at the empire's court. And around the city the record maps the rest of Judah into its villages, Kiriath-arba and Dibon and Ziklag and Lachish and Azekah, settled “from Beersheba all the way to the Valley of Hinnom.” The empty city had a population now, and the province had a map.

Chapter 12 first carries the priestly record forward in the same framed way, generation by generation: the priests and Levites who came up with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, then the high priests in succession, Jeshua, Joiakim, Eliashib, Joiada, Jonathan, Jaddua, and the heads of the priestly families in their days, down into the reign of Darius the Persian, recorded, the book says, “in the Book of the Chronicles.” The memoir's records reach past its author's own term of office; the keeping of the names mattered more than the governor's part in them. Then the lists give way to a day. For the dedication of the wall, the Levites were sought out from all their homes and brought to Jerusalem “to celebrate the joyous dedication with thanksgiving and singing, accompanied by cymbals, harps, and lyres.” The singers came in from their villages around the city. And before anyone climbed the wall, there was purification: “After the priests and Levites had purified themselves, they purified the people, the gates, and the wall.” Even the stones were consecrated before they were celebrated.

Then Nehemiah's own voice returns, and the dedication is his to describe. “Then I brought the leaders of Judah up on the wall, and I appointed two great thanksgiving choirs.” One choir went right, along the top of the wall toward the Dung Gate, Hoshaiah and half the leaders following, priests with trumpets, musicians with “the musical instruments prescribed by David the man of God,” and at its head a figure this series knows well: “Ezra the scribe led the procession.” It climbed the steps of the City of David, passed above the house of David, and came to the Water Gate on the east. The second choir went the other way: “The second thanksgiving choir proceeded to the left, and I followed it with half the people along the top of the wall,” past the Tower of the Ovens to the Broad Wall, over the Gate of Ephraim and the Jeshanah Gate and the Fish Gate, past the towers of Hananel and the Hundred, all the way to the Sheep Gate, where the building had begun. Two processions, circling a finished wall in opposite directions, singing.

They met where they were always going to meet. “The two thanksgiving choirs then stood in the house of God,” Nehemiah with them and half the officials, and the choirs sang out under their director. “On that day they offered great sacrifices, rejoicing because God had given them great joy.” “The women and children also rejoiced, so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard from afar.” The fox joke had been answered at distance. That same day, men were appointed over the storerooms for the supplies, contributions, firstfruits, and tithes, and the portions for the priests and Levites were gathered in from the fields, the record says, “because Judah rejoiced over the priests and Levites who were serving.” The service ran as David and his son Solomon had prescribed, and the daily portions flowed: “in the days of Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, all Israel contributed the daily portions for the singers and gatekeepers.” Wall dedicated, city filled, house supplied, covenant working. It is the highest point the book reaches, and the memoir lets it stand in full sound before it tells what happened when its author went back to Persia.

title: Remember Me, O My God
subtitle: Nehemiah 13:1–31
description: The governor returns to find Tobiah in the storeroom, the Levites in their fields, and the Sabbath for sale, and ends his book with a prayer.
paragraphs: The last chapter opens with the book of the Law doing again what it did at the Water Gate. The Book of Moses was read aloud in the hearing of the people, and in it they found the passage that no Ammonite or Moabite should ever enter the assembly of God, “because they had not met the Israelites with food and water, but had hired Balaam to call down a curse against them,” although, the text remembers, “our God had turned the curse into a blessing.” The people acted on what they heard and excluded all of foreign descent from Israel. Then the memoir turns back, with a phrase that explains everything that follows: now before this. Before this reading, while the governor was away, Eliashib the priest, who had charge of the storerooms of the house of God and was a relative of Tobiah, “had prepared for Tobiah a large room” in the temple courts, a large room where the grain offerings and frankincense and temple articles had been kept, and the tithes prescribed for the Levites, singers, and gatekeepers. Tobiah the Ammonite, the man of the fox joke and the unsealed letter, had been given an apartment in the house of God. “While all this was happening, I was not in Jerusalem, because I had returned to Artaxerxes king of Babylon in the thirty-second year of his reign.” Some time later Nehemiah obtained leave from the king and came back.

What he found, he dealt with in person. “Then I discovered the evil that Eliashib had done on behalf of Tobiah by providing him a room in the courts of the house of God.” “And I was greatly displeased and threw all of Tobiah’s household goods out of the room.” He ordered the rooms purified and had the articles of the house of God restored, with the grain offerings and the frankincense. Then the second discovery, the covenant's collapse at its foundations: the portions for the Levites had not been given, and so the Levites and singers “had gone back to their own fields” to feed themselves, and the service of the house stood empty. Nehemiah rebuked the officials with the covenant's own sentence turned into an accusation: “Why has the house of God been neglected?” He gathered the Levites and singers back and stationed them at their posts, all Judah brought the tithe of grain, new wine, and oil into the storerooms, and he appointed treasurers over them, men, the record notes, “considered trustworthy.” Then the refrain sounds: “Remember me for this, O my God, and do not blot out my deeds of loving devotion for the house of my God and for its services.”

The Sabbath was broken just as openly. In those days Nehemiah saw men in Judah treading winepresses on the Sabbath, bringing in grain and loading it on donkeys, with wine, grapes, and figs, all kinds of goods coming into Jerusalem on the Sabbath day, and men of Tyre who lived in the city importing fish and merchandise and selling them on the Sabbath to the people of Judah in Jerusalem itself. He rebuked the nobles: “What is this evil you are doing,” he asked them, profaning the Sabbath day. “Did not your forefathers do the same things, so that our God brought all this disaster on us and on this city?” “And now you are rekindling His wrath against Israel by profaning the Sabbath!” Then he used the wall. When the evening shadows fell on the gates just before the Sabbath, he ordered the gates shut and kept shut until the Sabbath was over, and posted his own servants at them so no load could enter. Once or twice the merchants camped outside the wall to wait out the day, and he warned them in person: “Why are you camping in front of the wall? If you do it again, I will lay hands on you.” From that time they did not return on the Sabbath. He set the Levites, purified, to guard the gates and keep the day holy, and prayed the refrain again: “Remember me for this as well, O my God, and show me mercy according to Your abundant loving devotion.”

Last, the marriages, the covenant's first clause and its hardest. In those days he saw Jews who had married women from Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab, and the evidence was in the children's mouths: “Half of their children spoke the language of Ashdod or of the other peoples, but could not speak the language of Judah.” What Nehemiah did is recorded in this telling exactly as he recorded it himself, neither softened nor celebrated: he rebuked them and called down curses on them; he beat some of these men and pulled out their hair. Then he made them swear before God: “You must not give your daughters in marriage to their sons or take their daughters as wives for your sons or for yourselves!” His argument was Israel's own history at its highest point: “Did not King Solomon of Israel sin in matters like this?” Solomon, loved by his God, made king over all Israel, and “yet foreign women drew him into sin.” And the rot had reached the priesthood itself: one of the sons of Jehoiada, son of Eliashib the high priest, had become a son-in-law to Sanballat the Horonite. “Therefore I drove him away from me.” His prayer over that one is aimed the other way from his own refrain: “Remember them, O my God, because they have defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites.”

The memoir's summary of the reforms is brief. “Thus I purified the priests and Levites from everything foreign, and I assigned specific duties to each of the priests and Levites.” He arranged the wood offering at its appointed times, and the firstfruits. Readers of this series will notice that the neglects Nehemiah found on his return, starved Levites, a trafficked Sabbath, foreign wives, are the very charges pressed in the disputations of Malachi, whose book stands in this same returned community; the two books are neighbors, and the telling leaves them so, inventing no meeting between the men. Then the governor signs off his book the way he has punctuated it throughout, not with a triumph but with a request. The last line of Nehemiah is a prayer, and the telling ends where he ended: “Remember me, O my God, with favor.”
